rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The elution window and resolutions will guide subsequent gradient and temperature adjustments.
The maximum CRF is already achieved, so shorten the gradient while holding temperature and endpoints fixed to test whether full resolution can be retained in a faster method.
Test the next shorter gradient to establish the speed–resolution boundary. The critical pair is close to the resolution threshold at 8 minutes, which remains a maximum-CRF fallback.

Test whether higher temperature changes selectivity enough to resolve the critical pair in the faster gradient. Holding the gradient fixed isolates the temperature effect; injection 2 remains a fully resolved fallback.

Return to the fully resolving 8-minute gradient and test a moderate temperature increase for faster elution. This should avoid the severe early-pair compression seen at 60 C while testing whether the critical middle pair retains adequate resolution.

Trim the gradient window while keeping its slope close to the fully resolving 50 C method. This should reduce time spent before the first peak and shorten elution while largely preserving critical-pair resolution.

Shift the gradient window upward at unchanged slope and temperature to shorten elution further. Monitor both the early pair and the marginally resolved middle pair for losses caused by reduced initial retention.
Slightly reduce gradient steepness to restore the middle pair’s resolution while retaining the faster start of injection 7. This should offer a shorter fully resolved separation than injection 6.

Explore a much steeper gradient at lower temperature to see whether the middle pair separates again after an elution-order reversal. The low starting organic fraction protects early retention, and injection 8 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Raise the starting organic fraction while reducing the gradient slope relative to injection 9. This tests whether altered initial retention improves the middle pair while the shallower slope spreads the late pair in a very short separation.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to alter middle-pair selectivity, with a shallower slope that may also resolve the late pair. Monitor early retention closely because the first peak may approach the unretained region.

Return to the successful 50 C selectivity with a narrower, shallower gradient to compensate for the higher starting organic fraction. This targets full resolution in a shorter separation than injection 8 while avoiding the nearly unretained first peak seen in injection 11.

Slightly flatten the gradient relative to injection 12 to increase the critical middle pair’s resolution margin. This tests a more robust maximum-CRF method while keeping all peaks well within the 10-minute scoring threshold.

Explore whether a further upward window shift resolves the remaining middle pair in the fast, low-temperature regime. This risks early-pair compression, but could substantially shorten the separation; injection 12 remains the fastest maximum-CRF fallback.

Test a narrower gradient at moderately lower temperature to preserve early-pair separation at the higher starting organic fraction. The shallower slope targets the middle pair, seeking a faster fully resolved method than injection 12.

Test a much shallower gradient in the fast, low-temperature region, backing down the starting organic fraction to protect the early pair. This probes whether the middle pair can regain full resolution through a selectivity change while keeping elution short.

Halve the gradient slope at fixed starting composition and temperature to improve the remaining critical pair. The final hold may delay the last peak, but the previous run suggests enough time margin to retain maximum CRF if full resolution is achieved.

Use a slightly shallower slope than injection 8 in a shorter programmed gradient to preserve full resolution with additional margin. The 0.60 endpoint remains above the previously observed last-peak elution composition, limiting the risk of delayed hold elution.

Refine around the fastest maximum-CRF method with a shallower gradient to strengthen middle-pair resolution. This should preserve early-pair separation and keep the last peak comfortably below the time-penalty threshold.

Increase the endpoint one grid step from injection 18 to test a faster separation near the middle-pair resolution boundary. Injection 12 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method if this steeper gradient loses full resolution.

Raise temperature one step from injection 20 to test whether improved middle-pair selectivity restores full resolution while shortening elution. Monitor the early pair carefully because higher temperature previously compressed it.

Lower both gradient endpoints from injection 21 to strengthen early-pair retention while preserving slope and temperature. This tests whether the early pair can recover full resolution without sacrificing the resolved middle pair.

Return to 50 C and preserve injection 19’s fully resolving slope while shortening the programmed gradient to four minutes. Its last peak eluted at approximately 0.48 organic fraction, so a 0.55 endpoint should retain full elution within the gradient.

Shorten the programmed gradient while preserving injection 18’s slope through the critical middle pair, then use the hold to elute the later compounds. This tests whether a two-minute gradient can retain maximum CRF, although the last peak may elute later than in injection 18.

Use a shallower gradient at 55 C to recover the early-pair resolution lost in injection 21 while preserving middle-pair separation. The maximum CRF is already secured; this final run tests an alternative fully resolved method at higher temperature.
